pedagogy.summary: The general principle that multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number n gives an equivalent fraction, and WHY: splitting each of the b parts into n equal pieces makes n×b pieces in the whole and n×a shaded, so the same amount is renamed with a finer counting-unit — the whole and the shaded magnitude are unchanged. This extends to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100) and is the same as multiplying the fraction by n/n, a name for 1.
bestPractices: Justify with re-partition: each part becomes n parts, so both counts grow ×n while the magnitude is fixed — the point does not move.
Generalise from many worked cases to the statement a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) (IES: any fraction can be written infinitely many equivalent ways).
Frame the move as multiplying by n/n = 1, so the value cannot change.
Apply directly to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100) as a bridge to decimals.
Confront the additive error head-on — multiplying is repeated re-partitioning; adding a constant is not.
keyRepresentations: Area model re-partitioned (each part → n parts)
Ratio table of numerators and denominators
commonMisconceptions: Additive equivalence — adding the same number to top and bottom keeps it equal (IES whole-number thinking)
Whole-number bias — (n×a)/(n×b) 'must be bigger' because the numbers are bigger (4/6 > 2/3)
Believing the value must change because 'you did something to it'

learn.summary: Learners understand WHY multiplying numerator and denominator by the same whole number n (n ≥ 1) gives an equivalent fraction: splitting each of the b parts into n equal pieces makes n×b pieces in the whole and n×a shaded, so the SAME magnitude is renamed with a finer counting-unit. This is the same as multiplying by n/n, a name for 1, so the value cannot change. It extends to tenths and hundredths (3/10 = 30/100). The central contrast is with the additive error: adding a constant to top and bottom is not re-partitioning and in general changes the amount (the only exception is a fraction equal to 1, such as 2/2 → 3/3); for example, adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator turns 2/3 into 3/4, which is larger, not equal.

activities.title: Rename the same amount: fix the shaded length, change the labels
feedback: If both counts grew but the shaded length stayed put, you have renamed the same amount — that is why 2/3 = 4/6.
If you changed only one part (just the top or just the bottom), re-cut EVERY part instead: splitting each piece changes both the shaded count and the total count together.
If the additive bar (3/4) visibly reached past the 2/3 strip, you have shown that adding 1 to each part is not equivalence — it moves you to a bigger amount.
To check the value is unchanged, ask: did I split each part into equal pieces (keeps the amount), or did I add extra amount (changes it)?
activities.rationale: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts, so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; holding a fixed magnitude while the labels change makes the invariance concrete and directly confronts the additive whole-number error. Paper strips are approximations of ideal flat regions, so the teaching point is the preserved shaded magnitude, not the paper itself.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Shade 2/3 of a bar (or mark 2/3 as a point on a number line) and keep that shaded length physically fixed — e.g. with a strip of coloured paper laid over the bar.
Subdivide every third into 2 equal pieces, then 3, then 4, and each time count the total pieces and the shaded pieces.
Record the sequence of names for the SAME shaded length: 2/3 → 4/6 → 6/9 → 8/12, and alongside each write the equation ×2, ×3, ×4 applied to both numerator and denominator.
State in your own words why the shaded amount never moved: each part was re-cut into more, smaller pieces, so both counts grew together while the whole and the shaded magnitude stayed the same.

Now test the additive move: change 2/3 by adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator to get 3/4. Shade 3/4 on an identical bar and lay it against the 2/3 strip. Observe that 3/4 reaches further — it is a different, larger amount.
Explain the difference out loud: multiplying re-cuts the same whole; adding a constant to each part does not re-cut anything, so here (and for any fraction not equal to 1) it lands on a new amount.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying numerator and denominator by a whole number n (n ≥ 1) re-partitions the same whole into finer equal parts, renaming a fixed magnitude; adding the same number to each is not re-partitioning and changes the amount (unless the fraction equals 1). Multiplying by n/n is multiplying by 1.

activities.title: Overlay check: is 4/6 bigger than 2/3?
feedback: If the two marks land on the same point, you have shown 4/6 = 2/3 despite the larger numbers.
If you expected 4/6 to be bigger, count the piece size: sixths are half the size of thirds, so 4 of them equal 2 thirds.
2/2 = 1, and multiplying any amount by 1 leaves it unchanged — that is the whole reason the rule works.
activities.rationale: Directly addresses whole-number bias (that scaled-up numbers 'must be bigger') by making the equal point/length visible on a common whole and tying it to multiplication by 1.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Place 2/3 and 4/6 on a shared number line (or overlay two identical strips, one cut into thirds with 2 shaded, one cut into sixths with 4 shaded).
Decide whether 4/6 lands on the same point as 2/3 or further along.
Explain why 4/6 is NOT bigger even though 4>2 and 6>3: there are more pieces, but each is smaller, so the total shaded amount is the same.
Connect this to multiplying by 2/2: state what 2/2 equals and why multiplying by it cannot change the value.
activities.intendedInsight: A larger numerator and denominator do not imply a bigger amount when both were scaled by the same factor — the pieces are correspondingly smaller, so the magnitude is unchanged.

activities.title: Generalise and bridge to tenths and hundredths
feedback: If each generated fraction matches 3/5 on your diagram, you have produced genuine equivalents, not just applied a step.
For 3/10 = 30/100, each tenth was cut into 10 hundredths: 10× as many pieces, each a tenth the size, same amount.
If you can say the factor (here 10/10 = 1) and why it preserves value, you understand the rule rather than just the procedure.
activities.rationale: Year 5 pupils identify, name and write equivalent fractions including tenths and hundredths; generalising from several verified cases to the symbolic statement supports durable understanding and the decimal bridge.
sourceClaims: In Year 5 (age 9–10) pupils identify, name and write equivalent fractions of a given fraction, represented visually, including tenths and hundredths.
learnerActions: Generate three fractions equivalent to 3/5 and verify each with a strip or number-line diagram.
State the general rule in words and symbols: a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) for any whole number n ≥ 1, and explain why it holds (re-partition each part into n).
Write 3/10 as hundredths: 3/10 = 30/100. State what you multiplied by (10/10) and why the value does not change.
Explain how this renaming into hundredths helps when working with decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The equivalence rule generalises to any whole-number factor n ≥ 1 and to the tenths↔hundredths renaming that underpins decimals; the justification (re-partition = multiply by n/n = 1) is the same every time.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: Jo vs Sam
feedback: Jo is right: 2/3 = 4/6. Multiplying both by 2 splits each third into two sixths — twice as many parts, each half the size — so the shaded amount and the whole are unchanged; it is the same point renamed, and ×2/2 is multiplying by 1.
Sam is wrong: adding 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator turns 2/3 into 3/4, a different, larger amount, because he is not re-partitioning the same whole.
If you endorsed Sam, place 2/3 and 3/4 on one line: they are different points. Adding shifts the amount; splitting each part keeps it.
If you said 4/6 > 2/3 because the numbers are bigger, overlay them: same point. More pieces, each smaller — same total.
If you only said 'do the same to both' without mentioning re-partitioning or the fixed amount, add the reason: each part is cut into more equal pieces, so the magnitude is preserved.
activities.rationale: A two-tier predict-explain task is proposed to discriminate genuine magnitude-preserving understanding from procedural recall and from the additive and whole-number-bias misconceptions; requiring the reason before observation is the intended diagnostic element. The cited claim supports the misconception content, not the format's efficacy.
sourceClaims: Equivalence is produced by re-partitioning the same quantity into finer equal parts (four pizzas among eight children: 4/8 = 2/4 = 1/2), so any fraction has infinitely many equivalent names; the additive 'add the same number to top and bottom' error is whole-number thinking, and treating numerator and denominator as separate whole numbers underlies errors like 3/8 > 3/5.
learnerActions: Read the claim: Jo says 2/3 = 4/6 (she multiplied top and bottom by 2); Sam says 2/3 = 3/4 (he added 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator). Before drawing, PREDICT with a reason whether 2/3 and 3/4 land on the same point.
Place 2/3, 4/6 and 3/4 on one shared number line (or overlay identical strips) and observe where each falls.
Decide who is right and justify: explain why multiplying keeps the amount but adding does not.

Answer the probes: Why does multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by 2 give twice as many parts but the same amount of chocolate? When you write 2/3 as 4/6, are you multiplying by 2 or by 2/2 — and what is 2/2? Is 3/4 bigger, smaller or equal to 2/3 — prove it on a line?
activities.intendedInsight: Equivalence is renaming a fixed magnitude by re-partitioning (multiplying by a form of 1); adding 1 to each part of 2/3 lands on a different, larger amount (3/4). Stating the reason before checking exposes whether the understanding is genuine.

constraints: A reference display of ×n families (tap 2/3 → 4/6, 6/9, 8/12 with ×n annotations) aids recall but does not let the learner enact the magnitude-preserving re-partition; use it as a support, not the main teaching move.

Recognition/selection tasks (choose which fraction equals 3/5; match ×n pairs; fill in 3/10 = ?/100) are useful for testing the rule and surfacing the additive distractor, but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own re-partition explanation — pair them with a construction or spoken justification.

When using paper strips or cutouts, treat them as approximations of ideal flat regions (real paper has slight thickness); the point is the preserved shaded magnitude, so keep the shaded length physically fixed when comparing names.
Correct the 'multiply only one part' error at the model: both numerator and denominator must change together because every part is re-cut; changing one alone is not equivalence.

A live, draggable subdivision slider with a linked ×n equation and a colour change on the additive move is one way to make the mechanism visible; it is an optional interaction example, not a requirement — the same insight can be reached with paper strips and a number line. Comparative efficacy between these media is not established by the sources.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source diagnostic states Sam adds 1 to the numerator and 1 to the denominator to get 2/3 = 3/4; the audited arithmetic is correct (2/3 ≈ 0.667 < 3/4 = 0.75, so Sam is wrong; 2/3 = 4/6 exactly). No arithmetic error found in the migrated examples.

The source IES claim quotes 'errors like 3/8 > 3/5' as a stated misconception (the true relation is 3/8 < 3/5); it is retained verbatim and framed correctly as an error, never presented to learners as true.
The National Curriculum source is marked unverified in the original; the tenths/hundredths age framing is retained as cited but not independently re-checked here.

The original 'directly defeats'/'cannot animate'/'best grasped not by dialogue' style claims about formats have been softened to scoped affordances; comparative efficacy of any single interaction format is not established by the sources.

The keyRepresentations 'ratio table' is not a standalone activity; the ×n sequence recording in activity 1 captures the same numerator/denominator tabular pattern. A dedicated ratio table could be added if a distinct representation is wanted.

assess.poeTask: Before drawing: Sam claims adding 1 to the top and bottom keeps a fraction the same, so 2/3 = 3/4. Ask the child to PREDICT, with a reason, whether 2/3 and 3/4 land on the same point on a number line. The reason stated before observing is the diagnostic part. Then place both on a shared line (or overlay strips): 3/4 sits to the right of 2/3, refuting the additive rule — while 2/3 and 4/6 coincide exactly.
probeDeeper: Why does multiplying top and bottom by 2 give twice as many parts but the same amount of chocolate?
When you write 2/3 as 4/6, what are you really multiplying 2/3 by — is it 2, or is it 2/2? What is 2/2?
Sam's method turned 2/3 into 3/4. Is 3/4 bigger, smaller, or equal to 2/3? Prove it on a line.
Write 3/10 as hundredths. What did you multiply by, and why doesn't the value change?
assess.correctAnswer: Jo is right: 2/3 = 4/6. Multiplying both by 2 splits each third into two sixths — twice as many parts, each half the size — so the shaded AMOUNT and the whole are unchanged; it is the same point renamed (and ×2/2 is multiplying by 1). Sam is wrong: adding 1 to each turns 2/3 into 3/4, a different, larger amount, because he is not re-partitioning the same whole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Additive equivalence — 'you can add the same number to top and bottom and it stays equal, so 2/3 = 3/4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place 2/3 and 3/4 on one number line to show different points; contrast splitting each part (×) with shifting the amount (+)
errorPatterns.distractor: Sam is right too — adding 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom keeps the fraction the same
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Endorses Sam, or says both methods are fine

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias — 'Jo changed it: 4/6 is bigger than 2/3 because 4>2 and 6>3'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Overlay 2/3 and 4/6 on strips / a shared line — same length, same point; multiplying by 2/2 is multiplying by 1
errorPatterns.distractor: Jo changed the fraction — 4/6 is bigger than 2/3 because the numbers are bigger
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the value grew after multiplying both parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplying only one part — thinks doubling just the top (or just the bottom) gives an equivalent
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show on the model that splitting each part changes the count of shaded parts AND the total — both numbers must move together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: When asked to check or generate another case, changes one part only

responseLevels.gap: Endorses the additive method, or says multiplying changes the value (bigger numbers = bigger amount); offers no magnitude-preserving reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Explains ×n as re-partitioning each part into n — both counts grow while the whole and shaded magnitude stay fixed (same point renamed) — shows adding moves the point, and transfers the reasoning to tenths → hundredths.
responseLevels.partial: Knows the ×n rule and picks Jo, but justifies only procedurally ('you do the same to both') without the re-partition / same-magnitude explanation, or cannot say why adding fails — listing the steps without relating parts to the whole.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Jo says 2/3 = 4/6 because she multiplied the top and the bottom by 2. Sam says 2/3 = 3/4 because he added 1 to the top and 1 to the bottom. Who is right? Explain, using a picture or a number line, WHY that method keeps the fraction the same and the other one doesn't.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The correct child links ×n to re-partitioning that preserves magnitude and explains why adding fails. A child with the additive misconception endorses Sam or treats both methods as equally valid; a whole-number-bias child says 4/6 > 2/3 because the numbers are bigger. It is hard to give the magnitude-preserving reason without genuine understanding, and hard to endorse Sam if you hold it.
